title: "Papa Jack" Laine and Mrs. "Papa Jack" Laine Interview, 1960-05-23
interviewee: "Papa Jack" Laine and Mrs. "Papa Jack" Laine

blocks.x: Dr. D dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear

Let's get down which issue this is. That's May the 15th, just last week, isn't it? Yeah. Yeah, I didn't get that. Times-Picayune. Yeah, Times-Picayune Sunday, May 15th. I wouldn't have knew it either. My daughter told me. In the amusement section.
Yeah, she said to me, did you see the... I said, no. She said, well, you... and I come back...
That same old instrument was in the First War.
She said, well, you're on the back of your radio program. She said, it's on the next page. So that's how I come and I got it. He didn't know nothing about it either.
No, I wouldn't have known nothing about it. The only time I get a chance to look at the paper when I've not got any... My hats are soaking and they're getting dry. Then I have a little time.
That's... They're fine with me. How was the parade yesterday?

Oh, boy, wonderful. You didn't go over there? No, I was wishing I could go over there. I wish I had come over there. I wish I had now too. I would have sent you home on your head. Oh, man, oh, man. Beer, whiskey and wine was bloated.
I can't take all that stuff. Did they have a band?
Did they have a band? They had music? Oh, no, no. I belong to one of the companies that did that parade. But didn't they have any music? No, Crockett. See, I belong to that. Did they have any music?
They had music!
Not about... only about 15 bands.
You see here, you know what you tell me? They tell you the truth.
You and your...
I thought you said, did I play? Oh, no, I knew you didn't play. Uh-uh. No, I knew you wouldn't play. They weren't a chance.
We wanted to ask you again, Mr. Lane, about some of the very... Now, look. Now, look.
Now, look. Can you say Jack Lane? Yeah.
Can you? We'll call you Jack Lane and Popper Lane.
That's right. That's right. Popper Lane either wanted to. Now, what's on your mind?
I wanted to ask about that very first drum you got when your father bought those flags and the drum up at the exposition. Yes. That's what you told us about.

Yes. Sugar and Cotton Exposition. Well, I had a small little drum, you know, like the Christmas toy drums, you know. Yes. And when the exposition broke up, they were selling out everything there. And, of course, my old man bought me a field drum.
One of the big high ones.

Yeah, one of those 18 inches. Well, you know. Well, with that thing, and one of our friends, one of my friend's boyfriends, he's daddy works up there also, you know. And they got lots of flags. See? We used them flags when we used to go around the street playing. Yeah. You know, a bunch of kids playing. Well, that's how I come to pick up on drums. See? Through that. And I began to organize a field band. Remarkable well. All them nickel tin flutes, you know, and stuff. Yeah. Went pretty good. So, after that, then I organized a string band. Made pretty good. Made a good record by that string band. Then I started an armed brass band. I got all the kids that played instruments, brass instruments, blowing instruments, see. So, I began to have them all to come around the house. She nursed them. Oh, I don't know how many of them young ones she did. What are you talking about?
Oh, terrible bunch of them.

They used to come around, you know. And there was a fellow by the name of Perkins. You might have heard of him. Dave Perkins. Yes. You heard of him? Yes. Well, he was a wonderful. Oh, he was a fine musician. Oh, you couldn't take it away from him. He used to show these kids, come around with me and show these kids how to hold the instruments, and how to blow the instruments, you understand. And I'd be holding the hoistlets right on, right on in my basement.
See? That first band you had with all the flags, was that right after that exposition they had up in Audubon Park?
Oh, it burst up. The exposition was broke up. Yeah, that was right after that.
Yes.
They stole everything. Yes. They stole everything there, you know.
Everything. Did you ever see that exposition? Did you ever go up there to those buildings and see?
No. No, I never saw it. No, I never seen it. No. Where were you living then? On Spain Street. On Spain. Yeah. I never did go up there, no. Never did?
About how old were you then?
I was too young at that time too, you know.
Well, see, that exposition was over in 1885, I think. You were born. 85 or 84? 84, along in there. 84.
84, I believe. Now, I... You were born when? 75. 21st day of September. On the 21st day of September in 1873. So you'd be about 11 years old.
Exactly.

11. Exactly. Exactly. Exactly. Exactly. And, well, of course, we started out then, you know, and I got very interested in it. And so the rest of the kids all got interested in it, you see. Yeah. So, we started. Then, when I started this field band, these political rallies used to go around, you know. Yeah. You know. You'd praise, you know, you understand, with brooms, you know, and mucks, and all sorts of stuff like that. Yeah. Well, they hired our bunch of kids one time ago to play, you see. So we played. Played for them. We got five dollars a piece too, don't forget it. We played for them. And since that, then I kept on going on with music, you see. I got a couple of boys who could play chord here and a little bit, you know, and guitar and so on and so on. So I organized a string band. Then, as I tell you, following that, I organized a brass band. Then another. Then my son began to come up, you understand.
Yeah. Well, when were you married? Maybe your wife can tell us about that too. Where were you living, Mrs. Lane?
When, uh, when we... Do you want to move your chair over a little bit?
Then you can talk too. Because if you feel all right over there. If that's comfortable, if you want to get a more comfortable chair or something like that. No, no, that's all right.
I'm comfortable nowhere with that lady. When were you married?
Do you remember the year? Do you remember the year? You ought to...
June the 23rd of 1894. 1894.
Yeah. Of course, Mr. Lane was still, was already playing music when you were married.
He used to play them political meetings, field bands and so on.
Before you were married, he was already in music then.

Right. Well, I don't know before I got married, you know, anything about that. No, she don't know about that. But, uh, since we got married, when he belonged to that Drum and Major Corps, uh, that was around in 1895. Somewhere in that. Somewhere in 95.
Somewhere in 95, right. And in 94, I, uh, some of my boys went up to the St. Louis Exposition. Oh, yes.
You told us once. You didn't go yourself though.
I went up there, they asked me to come up there. I was up there for two or three weeks. Two weeks, I believe it was, wasn't it? Something like about two weeks.
Yeah, you went.

I was up there. But I had to get back on account of so much contracts coming in, you understand. I had to depend on her. You see? And I had this man, you know, Marlon, Lawrence Vega, running the band. He always has. Cornet players. Oh, a mockable cornet players. So was Richie Brunitz. Oh, very good.
How was Nick LaRocca in those days? Oh, brother.
Aye, aye, aye.

Here's a big article they got out on the... Another one? That's in the Tulane paper. He gave a lot of his things to Tulane. Of course, he tells them that he's the one that started jazz. Oh. Oh, oh, my God. That's awful. Well, let them have their fun.

Let them have their fun. Listen, how... There's a magazine section there when he was a couple of years old, I don't know how much, a couple of weeks ago. He states then that he had to hide a cornet that he had in the well in his home. Yes. How could he do such a thing? When the first... He didn't even know how to hold a cornet in his mouth when he played with... He used to sit in the Elmire Pleasure Ground... Well, he did. ...in the park. And Manuel Marlowe is the man that showed him how to blow the cornet.

He used to, you know, play, but not anywhere as good, you understand? So this Manuel Marlowe, one of the leaders of my band, I had a couple of bands, of course, the leaders in all these bands. I don't get it.
How they can tell such a thing?
Well, all the time, most of all, Nick used to come with Manuel Marlowe. And Manuel Marlowe used to show him how to finger and all that stuff and break him in on these...
And he had a number of all of them. On these numbers, you understand?
Yeah. See? So, uh... That he played. Then Nick got along with playing pretty bad. As you know, with his brass band. He got along pretty good with his connet.
Hold on, that's a shame after that. Well, that's... Your wife's telling about, you said he used to play funerals?

He said he did? Yes, there was a magazine article in the paper about that. And I will be willing. I'd go stand up anyways. I'd fight him to the last. Because he is a liar. Plain-faced liar. He didn't even know how to put the connet in his mouth at that time. When he first started to play, when he used to be at Elmire Pleasure Ground with him. And after that, he used to come to the house there on Charter Street and try to rehearse them. Manuel tried to show him how to play. Then after that, he used to leave them go in the parades. Yeah. But he couldn't play though. But he went in the parades, in the carnival parades with the horn. But not that he played. Because he couldn't play. Well... I can tell him that.

Of course, he began to improve a considerable lot. Yeah. But when I'd take him in the parades, I'd pay him as well as I paid the rest of the men. So he couldn't play much then? Well, he couldn't play very much, no. In fact, whether he didn't know how to play these numbers or not, I don't know. But eventually he did. He got onto all of that stuff, you see. Then he began to play the connet pretty good. He played a pretty good trumpet.

That's another liar. That he... That Tiger Rag. He's another liar. He didn't write Tiger Rag. No, he didn't. No, not half of it, no. Because he played... And Alcide Nunes, they used to call it plurine and meatballs, the same thing. And he's the one that played it, but not La Raffin.

I'm different, putting a name from meatball, plurine, keep a shuffling and all that sort of stuff. I don't know how they can get the liars. But you can bet all he writes and all he has written and all he has said.
He never mentions him. He never mentions him. He never mentions him. Not once, does he? No, not, no. No, you bet not.
Only they'd get together and practice this stuff, you understand? Of course, you know, they'd knock out a full tune. With chorus and everything else to it.
Did you play Tiger Rag then with your band long before La Rocca, you say? Sure.
He called out a Liberty Stable Blues, I believe, or something like that is.
No, I believe that's something else. No, that was something else, I think. That's something else, Stable Blues.
That was Yellis, Yellis too, and Yellis and Paquet.
That's the ones for Tiger Rag, Paquet and Yellen Nunes. They made it up, you think?
Yes!
They had a big cold scramble in Chicago, New York. Oh, I read about that. You remember that? Yeah. Had him, had, I'll see, have a Yellen Nunes arrested.
Well, that's just how that happened, you see? Now, of course, uh... But he is a liar.
Holy, he's a liar.

The time that, the time La Rocca went up there, now I'm not sure, I'm only saying this because it's so safe. It was told to me. That some fellow would come up in a parade we were playing, from north, and wanted to know about musicians. Yes. And now, it seems to me, now I'm not saying that I know about this, but it was told to me. The Rocca then represented himself as the main squeeze.
It was one of your bands, I heard, though.
Yes, played in my band.
That's what I heard, too.

Yes. And, uh, of course, it happened to be close to a Mardi Gras. And I had three bands out that year. And, uh, well, little Brunus, Abby, he was a pretty fair corner player. It was then at that time, too. He was picking up mighty nice, very nice. Well, he sends Abby Brunus in each place to play that carnival parade. While he went around scouting, I guess, to get members to go north with, see? Now, he claims he went first there, to went up north first. No. I believe Tom Brown was a man who went up north first. I think he did, too.
I believe he went a year before or so.

I believe Tom Brown went up. Because, uh, we used to speak about these things, you know. And, uh, after that, he went up. Then, after that, my boy took each band up there, see? And, uh, that's how they come to be up north. You understand? In fact, I couldn't go. I really couldn't go because I had too much contract, too many contracts, you understand, to fill, see? And, uh, you can believe me or not. I was speaking to a man the other day. Well, you can say and stand up to say you played five jobs, six, five, and six jobs in one day, I believe you're going playing. That's right. You're going strong. Yeah, that's right. And that sounds pretty much like a lie. But I can tell you every one of them jobs that I played and for whom? That was at carnival time? During a carnival, Mardi Gras day. Happened on a Mardi Gras day. Dr. Cavado hired me from seven to nine. I'm going to explain these things to you, how I come to play them jobs. He hired me from seven to nine, advertising antiseptic pills and all that of drugs. He had a whole bunch of kids with them boxes around them, you understand? And with all the advertisement on the drugs advertisement, see? Now, I had a furniture wagon. We used to go around in a furniture wagon. And the signs on that furniture wagon was for the Merriors with his ball. We played the Merriors with the ball at the same time I advertised. Now, after I played from, to nine o'clock, we get in this wagon and advertise the Merriors with his ball. Then I get up, at that time we have to be, it's no use, no talking at all. We had to be up at Cali Open St. George for ten o'clock. It was only nine o'clock, mind you. We had one hour only. We had to do some hustling. Well, we got up there and I played that Mardi Gras parade. After I finished playing that Mardi Gras parade, I had to play the View of Damascus on Frenchman and Decatur. I believe it was an hour or two there. We jumped in that wagon again and finished the Merriors with his ball. Finished advertising Merriors with the ball. It was time to get up to Cali Open St. Charles. We had to get something to eat on the fly. We were on time to get up there for the night parade. Cali Open St. Charles. I made that night parade. After the night parade, I played the Merriors with his ball.
What a day.
Nine o'clock, I started the Merriors with his ball. We were finished playing that night parade. It was only about, how was they say then, about five blocks we had a walk for the hall.
What kind of a band did you use for the ball? How big a... A brass band. A brass band played that too. Yeah, yeah. About what year was this? About what year? Oh, now I...
About what year? I really, I had a lot of records.
Yeah, I don't know.
Many records.

They got so bad in the trunk. When I built this place. When I built this place. I was nothing but roaches. I said, get rid of this. She turned them all out in the yard. I burned them up, I said, oh. You burned it all up then, huh?
I burned it up to just ashes. I burned it.
Well, they were...
Well, I didn't blame her because of the drawing roaches and all that sort of stuff, but there was some value for something there.

I got a swan book there with some... But this is another... Another big liar he's got here. Because she's pointed up. What's that then? In 1917. Ever there was a liar. That's the biggest liar he could ever tell.
He claims he started jazz about 1917.

In 1917. That's one big liar. Because he wasn't even playing music that I remember at that time. That's about when Mr. Wayne Quidditch. And I know when, because my grandson was born in 1917. And he's still living. Lance was born in 1917. Lance.
Lance, yeah.
And that's when he claimed he went to... He went up north with the band. Yeah.
Oh, God.
How can you make up the liars?
Well, I wanted to ask something about those funerals. You said Nick La Rocca didn't play any funerals, but did your band play for some of the funerals?
The who?
Funerals for.
David Croc at funerals.
He didn't know no more about playing the funeral than you.
No, but did you play the funeral?
Oh, did I? Sure did. Sure, there's his...
Sure did.
I played for the owls.
He belonged to David Croc.

I belonged to David. I played for them. I used to play all their dances, all their balls, all their parades. You leave Benevolent Association, I played all their parades and all their dances and all their... All their barrails, all their funerals.
Anyway. Did you play very many funerals? How often did they have a funeral that way with music? Oh, not very often, no.
No, I don't think they did. No. I don't think they did, really. I don't believe it. No. I don't believe it.
You know, when they used to play... When did they stop playing funerals with music? I mean, was this back in the 90s or was this back...
When did they start playing music for funerals? In what year? You don't remember?

I really don't. And I ain't gonna say I do because I don't. I don't know. Oh, I know he don't. He don't remember. I don't... I never paid that much mind outside of the records. I used to... I used to keep those records and the contracts. From whom, where, when and what. Keep them all in together. I had a trunk load of that stuff, I tell you.
I got this picture here.
I got this picture.
I had a trunk load of that stuff.
I got this picture. She put it all up.
Of La Rocca and Shields.
Well, do you remember whether it was back in the 90s or in... Oh, yeah.
Back in about the 90s.
Way back when you first started having a brass band.

Because in 1904, some of my boys played an artificial garden in St. Louis for the Grand View Portainal Hotel. It was an artificial garden. Yeah. An artificial garden, see. And I went up there, I believe, for two weeks, I think it was. They asked me to come up there. Now, there was only three of the boys went up there, my boys, but they had five in that band. They used two from up there. The piano player they used and the drum player from up there they used. See. Now, the carnet and the clarinet player and the bass player was from here, my men. They asked me to come up there one time, you know. I kind of managed to squeeze in to find a little time to go up there. And brother, you take it from me. When I left, you almost cried. And, uh... You know, at the time, not to speak about myself being wonderful on that, but I really was.
You had a good band on that band.

Oh, remarkable. And I couldn't feel the engagements. I'm going to tell you just right now, I couldn't feel the engagements. But did they have funerals about the time of the St. Louis trip? They were about winding up around that time in 1904. Yes, I believe it was about winding up around that time, funerals, yeah.
How big a band did you use for that, for the funerals? Ten or twelve.

Ten or twelve. And what kind of music did you play? All marches, dead marches, all funeral marches. All funeral marches. Our main piece was a piece they called Under Arms. And it was a march, it was a military march, at the same time you could use it for a burial march.
You had the music for that?
Oh, yes. You had the music. Oh, yes. I had the music for that, yeah.
Did you... I had music.
Now, you see, most of the band didn't read. Most of my boys didn't read. Only a couple of them did. See?
Yeah.

A couple of them did. Now, what I've learned was through Perkins. You know how I learned in the notes, it was through Perkins. See? Yeah. He'd teach me and show me just what to do and where to make my stops, where I make rows, where I have to beat before rows and so on. See? Well, then I got onto all of that very quick.

That's the same year that Alfred went to New York. He played. He was with Durante, my son. That's right. He was with Durante. Yes, sir. We got Durante's card. His wife, he never fails sending him a Christmas card every year. And when he died, he sent him a beautiful card. Jimmy Durante? Yes. Fact. Yes. In 17, Alfred Lane was with Durante in New York in the Alamo Cafe. So how could...
He wouldn't have...

I know one night, he'd come on TV, in the Rocker, with a whole lot of stuff. Yeah. And lawyer Kenner called my daughter. And her and him called up the station. And they told him what a liar he was and all that they didn't tell him. He picked up all these things and walked off the station and never seen them no more.
He quit right there.
And I'll give it to him. He give it to him in no... No. That was Arnold Leuco. Arnold Leuco, yeah.
Poor Nick LaRocca never played no funeral. He couldn't play a funeral.
He knows Arnold Leuco knows that the Rocker didn't.
He couldn't play a funeral. He didn't know. He knows it.
He knows it.
He knows it. Do you remember who some of the men were in your band back in those days that did play a funeral?
Do I remember some of them? You remember some of your men. I remember some of them. Back of the day. Yeah, you must remember a lot of them. Sure I do. Yeah. You must.
Most of them are dead. Yeah. There's only two of them living. You like to take Richard Brunish and Marlowe and... Jimmy Kennel just died.
Jimmy Kennel died too about two months ago.
Yeah, he just died. Most of them, the Brunish boys are living.
What about Chinka Martin? He's living. He's living. He's living. Oh yeah. He played with you in the old days.

Oh yeah. Here's a queer thing. This is a really coincidence. Yeah, it seems. I had a man by the name of Kaskrow playing bass with me, you know. And he took very sick. And that takes me one of them Wild West show jobs. And I needed a tuba player. See? So Kaskrow couldn't play. He was sick. Down and out couldn't play. So I borrowed the horn from him. See? Yeah. And I stuck it in Chink's hand. I said, whether you know or not, I said, you're going to learn this thing. Yes or no? For me? You're going to learn it? He said, I don't know nothing about that. I said, you're going to learn it? Take it. He stood up there and he started pumping in it. Of course, the band drowned them. You know, false notes and all that. Drowned them. But don't you know that it was no time at all that Chink Martin could handle that bass as good, that bass horn as good as any man in this man's town? So I went to Kaskrow and I said, Joe, I said, you've all washed up. I said, how about selling me that tuba? He said, yeah, something sell it to you. Give me eight dollars for it. Give me eight dollars for it. Give it to Chink Martin. And brother, he made a tuba player. There ain't no question about it. Then I had this fella Alexander, Joe Alexander playing tuba with me too, you know. He was a pretty good tuba. He used to play a hurricane tuba. See?
Oh, yes. One of those. One of the guys.

Played one of them tubas. Now, his son too, you know. His son Manuel, the fella that's a professor today. He played with me too. He's living. Manuel, ain't he living? Who? Manuel Alexander. Manuel Alexander.
You told me you met him, yeah. I don't know. I've never seen him.
He's living, I believe, today.
A long time ago.
Well, he played with me too. He trained out to be a professor of music.
Yeah, he's teaching in some college. Oh, yeah. Then we're doing, isn't he? Yeah. Manuel.
Now, Ernest Stevens, he's living. He played with me too.
Yeah, Ernest Stevens. He come here.
He's from here.
Is he still here in town? Yeah. He's got his own home back in Gentilly somewheres. I got his address. I got his telephone number. Yes, we'd like to look him up sometime too.
Well, I was going to ask some more about the funerals. See?
There's the band. There's what they got.
Let's look at the picture first then. That's the picture. That's the group with Nick LaRocca. Yeah.
That's what you got here. And Tony, yes.
I think we saw that before when Johnny Wiggs was here. Yeah. Tony and Eddie Edwards.
Tony and Edwards. Tony and Eddie Edwards. LaRocca Nunes.
That's the... Or the Ragus. That's Yellow Nunes there, not Shields this time. Yellow Nunes, yeah. That's before Shields joined then. Yeah. What was that tape?
That was...

It says Chicago down here, I think, yes, on the picture. Some studio in Chicago. Yes, yeah. Yeah, I can't make out. L-A-G-U-E-R-R-E. French or Italian name or something. Used a piano, is that? An old style upright piano. He only used one Chinese symbol. Well, I was going to ask some more about those funerals. On the way back from the graveyard, did you still play slow music or what kind of music?
Oh no. Rough. Anything go long. Anything. Anything. Ragtime, anything. Long coming back.
Yeah.
The last barrel march we would play is when they put the body in the tomb. Or in the hole. Yeah. See. Then...
This is 20 years ago, this picture.

Then the minister or priest or whatever... He had that taken. He's held a ceremony over his body. They mean a Christian. Right after that we'd march all out, we'd walk out, not march, walk out to the gate of the cemetery and the organizations would form up right there. Then we'd start from there. See. We'd start right from there coming on back to the hall.
And the organization marched back with you then? Oh yes.
Bring the organization right back to the hall. Yeah. Oh yeah.

What organizations you said, the Crockett Fire Company and what other organizations did you charge for? Who else did you play for? The Davy Crockett and then who else? Who else had the funerals? Lee Benevolent.
Lee Benevolent. They were a very large organization. Was that on this side of the river or over there? No, over in Gretna. Over there. Over in Gretna, yeah. L-E-E.
Who? Lee. Lee, yeah.
L-E-E.
Yes. L-E-E.

Yes. I played the funerals over there. And I used to play also, there was a club over there, a very good club but it wasn't very strong, the Owls, they called themselves the Owls. They were out on the river bank. They had their clubhouse out on the river bank. They'd parties, funerals and the balls and all like that. I'd play for that, see? See? Then I played the Suburban Racetrack. That was my main spot, the Suburban Racetrack. Where was that? Over in McDonneville.
Over on the other side.

McDonneville, yeah. And Cramer's lot was in Algiers. They had them going, see? Yeah. And the Crescent Park was up in Gretna. See? Yeah. Well, I'd have bands put in there every Sunday or Saturday night in them three parks, regular. Regular. Races and all that sort of stuff at the Suburban Park I played. Oh yeah. Yeah.
You mentioned the Elmira pleasure ground too. Did you play there? Yeah. Elmira's, yeah. Every Sunday.
Every Sunday.
Oh yes, yes.
What did they have there? Picnics or what?
Picnics, yeah. Yeah. And a regular open pavilion.

Regular open pavilion, just for the little stuff. Top on it, shed over it, you know. And Mr. Foster had the ballroom right across from the... Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm.
That's Mr. Stevens. What's his name again? Ernie Stevens?
Yeah, Ernie Stevens, yeah, right here. And that's his two sons. They were in the service, too. And this here is Emil Christian and Tony Parenti.
She's only keeping this stuff since we moved back in this place.
That's Brown, Lopez. This is Loyal Canna.
You know I must have had some dope ones. Oh, I'm telling you, I have it.
I mean, I have newspaper cut in school. He comes every now and then he comes in town, too. Yeah, I got his picture about 20 years ago.
You see, the thing is, you know, you got the pictures before you to show you that it must have been sold. Must have been sold.
You gave him the gold record, yeah.

Must be positively sold. Because your pictures will show you. That's right. Yeah, yeah. When did you first start playing Funerals? When did you first start playing Funerals? When you first start playing Funerals. When I first, oh, now, I can't answer that because I really don't remember. No, he knows.
I really don't remember.
I don't remember. Can't answer it. Well, do you think?
But God only knows, I played them.

Played a lot of them, huh? I played them, all right. There's a lot of men who are living today that can bear me out to the truth with that. They're all over the river, lots of them. Right today, living. Did you play them for many years? Did you play Funerals for many, many years?
They didn't play music for funerals too long, did they?
No, no, no. No, I remember that. No, no, they didn't. No, they didn't. No, they cut that out. They cut it out.

They cut out them funeral marches out. out, I believe I'm pretty sure of that. Just a few years you played them. Huh? Just a few years, just a few years that you played the Funerals. Yeah, Funerals. Really? Yeah. Really? Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah.
Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah.

After I got started with the bands, you understand, got the bands are going pretty good. The first man, the first job that I got for Funerals Marches, I'll never forget that as long as I live, it was from that company. It was with the Davy Crockett. Yeah.
The fire company. Yeah. That was your first wife.
He's dead now. His name was Rap. The man's name was Rap. Yeah. Well, uh.
Happy Rap was the man's name.
His wife was fired to Bud Lai Canna. He come to me and I can't, I think, his wife is married to Bud Lai Canna.

One of the old men anyhow died. To Bud Lai Canna. Yeah, Bud, you know Bud, he said not to Rapp at all. Well, he said you can get over this stuff, I know you can. He's here. His picture, we got his picture here, Bud.
But his wife, that was her first husband.
Yeah, he's scared. Yeah, Rap was his husband. Happy Rap says you ain't scared at all, you're gonna do the job. I know.
Bud Lai Canna.

I mustered up the man and I got two men pretty good on reading, given the main parts. And believe me or not, brother, we went there. We went to town. Because the boys that I had liked his shield back, I say, Bucket and those fellas like that, you know. We got a, we got a little. The miniatures pop up on something, it seemed like you knew just what key and everything else you were gonna go into. It seemed to me that way now. I don't know, I might be wrong. But by God, they'd go right along with it. How much?
We got a letter from Gussie Miller when Pocket died. Oh yeah, Gussie's living too.
Gussie Miller's living too. Yeah, he sent us a nice letter.
How much did they pay you for those funerals? Three dollars. Three dollars a man. Were colored bands playing funerals when you started playing?
Colored bands was playing when you played? Oh yes.

Yes, it was two colored bands that I remember. Two colored bands only. And brass bands, but I don't remember any orchestra. Remember nothing like that. And the man that had the first band was, oh, I can't speak of his name now. But anyhow, he had a military band and believe me, he had a pretty good band.
They played funerals then too.
He played funerals too, yeah. All for colored people. I don't know how he could go. The colored people used to go wild on that, you know.
I don't know how a writer could say such things.

No matter what it was, what kind of band it was, they wanted a band at their funeral. I don't know. I think you say it. See? So, they had two that I remember. That's a good to remember of two colored bands. Brass bands. But I don't ever remember any orchestra. Because, uh...
Well, who do you think started playing, who do you think played funerals earlier? White bands or colored bands? Oh, I believe white bands.
Yes, I think of white bands, yeah. Did they have them before you started?
The funerals before you started? Oh, yes, yes, yes. They'd been playing funerals before then? Yes, yes, yes.

Sure it was. Yeah. Yeah. Now this man, Brookhoven, used to play to most of them funerals. A man by the name of Brookhoven, a German, used to play most of those funerals. See? I wonder, Stephen's daddy was playing drum in these bands. Brookhoven's band. Yeah.
Did they ever play any of the ragtime coming back? No. In those days? No. No.
No. No. There's straight marches coming back. Straight marches, yeah.
Do you remember the names of some of the marches?
No, I don't. I really don't. I really don't. I can't say I do, but I don't.
Did colored bands play straight music coming back? Did the colored bands play straight music or ragtime coming back? Do you remember?

Straight music. They did too? Yeah. I remember, oh I can't think of his name, not Oliver. Cutler's brother had a band. I remember his band because I heard his band play time and time again. See? And I had my band going on too, you know. My band was going on too. On the other side of the river? Vega, he used to show Vega too how to play. He used to have a finger in the corner. Who? Oh, this colored fellow. I can't think of his name now.
There was one man, the colored fellow had a band I heard of, Manuel Perez. Manuel Perez is a man. That's the man?
That's the man. Manuel Perez. That's the boy.
I mean Manuel had a good band.

He couldn't take it away from him. He was sort of a military band. He had a good band. Now there's only one band in this town that plays almost. Well, in fact, if you sit up, heard my band play and walk away and hear this colored band play, you'd hear my same stuff. What's his name? Paul Barbarian. Who? Barbarian. Barbarian. Barbarian. I guess that is. Barbarian. Barbarian. The same kind of stuff and almost the same temperature. They've got two, they've got two of those color bands as the same.
They both played for the Jazz at their auditorium one night. What's that other name of that other colored band?
I don't know, but that's when I discovered this Paul Barbario. I had his picture too.
I think you told me once before when we talked to you, it was George Lewis, I believe you said. Lewis, I believe Lewis, don't you know Lewis?
Lewis, the colored band, wasn't it Lewis?
The clarinet player, George Lewis, I think you told me before.
Oh, she's Barkay's brother, George Barkay.
Oh, I don't know about Barkay's brother. No, no. It was the two bands that played at the auditorium the night we were up there, the jazz club had
something. One of them sang that song.
The Saint Comes Marching In.
Yeah, I believe that was Lewis, yes.
Yeah, I believe it was. I had his picture, but I don't know.
There was a couple of bands up there that night. There was a couple of bands up there.
That's the type of music that you played when you were up there.

Yes. Yes, exactly. This bugbearer played. Exactly. I said, look here. I said, that ain't my stuff. Nothing in the world is. Same stuff to that thing. Now, I quit playing music right after War I, first war. Not some of them, most of them were drafted. One of them died in the Army. Well, they took some of the boys up there like, I'm going to explain it to you, and they made a band up there, you know. At the camp? Yeah, at the camp. At the camp. At the camp Beauregard. They sent down for me. And I was right busy, playing right along. So, they sent down for me. But I had a few extra men on the side. And I had to keep some of them jobs going. You understand why? Oh, most of them were gone. Yeah. Good luck, I used to have a few spares, don't you know, that I could fall on. Well, I went up there. They asked me to come up there. I went up there, you know. And I don't know what the major's name was anyhow. But no, anyway, they sent me my ticket. They sent me $50 a week in cake. All right, I went up there and I stayed up there for about seven weeks or something like that. And I couldn't stay any longer. So, just before I left, maybe a day or two, they were speaking about Armistice. You understand? But I left. And after that they did. They closed the place and turned it into a nigger camp. And they'd get you a colored camp. We used to make all kinds of money. We'd play for them while they were in the mess room. We'd play. We'd play for dances for them. One of the crazy boogers would put their hats out, you know. Make us dimes quartered and all that matter. We'd share. After we got done playing, we'd share $80, $10 a piece. That went on until I came back and kept playing with my band, you see. There was a couple that I had left, you see. And I stopped. And so I couldn't make the go, I stopped. All my good men were gone.
See.
So then I quit.

Can you tell us all the different occasions that would hire music when you were young? You once told me they used to have weddings and everything else. They'd always hire a band. What kind of parties? Yes.
Parties and band, weddings and stuff like that. Yes. Parties. I played a many, many long party. I, with top pollin spread out there, up in the Irish Channel. With top pollin spread over the mud.
Huh?
I played a many of them.
What do you think? I taught him, Mr. Russell. You met Mr. Russell?
I think one time you were talking with Chink Martin and you said that almost every wedding they'd always have a band in those days. Yes. Yes.
Almost every wedding. It was surprise parties. King parties. King parties. King K cutting outfits. So on and so on. Yes, it had music. This one had to do with your, uh,
Yeah. Oh no, that's all right.
That is had music.

Give you a little breeze. Oh! I have the mic pointed the other way. I don't think it'll pick up the sand. Uh, what other kind of parties did you play? Any other kind of special parties or anything else?

No, nothing but balls. The balls were the balls of course and picnics. Yes. Sure. But parties like that. Weddings and surprise parties and something like that. You know. How many nights a week did you work? Well, I'll tell you. Some weeks I'd be going putting air every night. Putting air every night. I'd be playing. Yeah. Every night. Every night. Even when I'd play at Millenburg. I'd play at Millenburg. I'd play at Millenburg. We'd start at Millenburg playing out there at nine o'clock in the morning. Understand on a Sunday. On Sunday. On Sunday. And after we'd play Millenburg, I had to go over the river with the bands and get them all to play parks, different parks over the river. See? After we got done playing at Millenburg. See? And we'd go over the river and play them parks. Look. I would play the parks up until twelve o'clock. Sometime extra hours over. One or two hours over. See? We'd play that. You know. Extra hours. See? And we'd play that. And I'll never forget as many days as I live. Those bands that organized after I organized color bands. They'd play in these camps almost close to one another. They'd say, you better play music. There are Lions Banders over there. Jack Lane's Banders over there. You probably better play good music. You say that to one another, you know. There was a nigga by the name of Green. He's dead. He used to tell me a whole lot of this stuff, too. He used to tell me a whole lot. None of the stuff they played, they used to copy off me. He said that. None of the stuff they played, they'd copy it off of my band. He used to tell them, you better play music. Jack Lane is over here to a line.

I was going to ask about some more of these tunes, like the Dixieland One Step, they call it. La Rocca put his name on all of those. Skeleton, Django, Fidgety Feet, Sensation. He claims he wrote all of those numbers. Do you remember any of those other tunes?
He wrote all of them numbers?
But he says all of those he wrote.
No, sir. No, sir. After he learned that stuff from us, he did this thing.
When did he start playing with you? Do you know about...
No, I really don't. I really don't. No, I don't.
Ask it on.
But...
Oh, that trash on there. That's a funny...

He came around, you know, and wanted to come into rehearsal once again and another, and so everything was all right, you know. Then he come out with us, playing jobs, you know, different jobs, and not pay him just as well as I pay the rest of the men.
See? I see you. It's nice to meet you. So...

Well, he kept on playing until... with me, until this Mardi Gras Day action happened, when he sent little Brunus in his place, Abbey Brunus, see? Now, when he sent Abbey Brunus in his place, of course, I didn't have... I believe it was about two, three bands I had out only that day. Understand? And I never had enough room to make another band to send out, which I had the band ready if they wanted it. Well, I could send it out. See? And Brunus happened to be in Bearville that day, and Rocker grabbed him, put him in his place to play the carnival parade. That's how he played.
Well, sometime Nick LaRocca told about that you used to have some of the men put potatoes in the horns. Do you remember that? Well...

The fellas that couldn't play? I'll tell you what happened. We played... We played for Martin Borman in the old St. Charles Hotel frame building. You understand? Yeah. And it was his campaign, running for mayor. My first daughter mayor. Was it Alfred put Limburger cheese in...
Martin Abraham's...
Martin Abraham's horn? Yeah.
All the skin, the team got the Limburger cheese, you know how nice that smells. He put that down in his...

He filled his heart up with Limburger cheese. Man, it smelled something horrible. Every time he'd blow in it, that... You know that odor. It'd knock you... Yeah, they used to put stuff in them. Them kids used to play. Every one of them. They were up to all kinds of stuff.
LaRocca talked like if you'd hire somebody sometime that couldn't play at all, you'd put a potato in the horn so they couldn't make any noise to hurt anything.
LaRocca did.
He said that you did that, I think. I did. Yeah, on some of the men that they couldn't play. Do you remember that? Ever putting potatoes in their horns so they couldn't play?
No, no, no. I remember playing jokes on men that played music.
Yeah.

That really played music. They said, fellas take it off, they don't take their socks off and shove it down. Yeah. That's all of that sort of stuff. Well, they used to play to miss them kids, you know. We were all youngsters then, you know. They were terrible. I had a handful to handle them. They were over home with her all the time, a whole bunch of them. I had a garret, a big open garret, you know. Had beds up in there. And when I'd take a job out of the city, I wouldn't trust them buggers. I'd make them come and stay by me. See? I'd get them up early in the morning, maybe five o'clock, maybe half past four train, leaving from the LNN or whatever road it was, early. Now, I'm just as sure as the almighty God in heaven, Joe Stevens is dead in his grave today. It's a mighty good thing that there were two trains going to Biloxi that morning. Stevens over slept, and simply missed the first train, and I just had time enough to go down to his house. He lived on Tulu, Tulu's, or St. Louis Street, near the Cedar. And the railroad, of course, was right up here, canal in the river. A few blocks. And get him out, and get him on time to get that train to make that job in Biloxi. As almighty God told. Overstepped himself. But when I come there, they were up. They were up. When I came there, the minute that train pulled out and I didn't see him there, you know, I said, well, I found out that there was another train followed pretty shortly. I said, let me see if I can make it. With God sending, I made it. I got Rag Baby Stevens out on time.
Is there anything else, Mrs. Lane, you could tell us about the old days when your husband had the bands? That you'd like to add?
I don't know.
You were married, you say, in 1894. Yes. Was Mr. Lane much older than you?
Yes, I was older than you.
Seven years. Seven years.

Oh, I muck with music before I started to play. Before I got married, you muck around a kid, you know, before I was married. I was already about 13 years old, so like that, when I started, you know. I had a drum. I believe it was old man Gilmore's boy. I bought it off of him, a Christmas toy, in other words. That was my first instrument. But the first good instrument came from the expedition. a field drum. They called it a field drum.
Did it have the ropes on it
or the rods? Yes, ropes. Ropes. And my first bass drum, the first bass drum that I got come from Salvation Army, it was roped.
Roped, too.
Leather tongues. It was roped.
What kind of flags did they get from the exposition? Do you remember what the flags were like?
All nations, nationalities.
All different.
Yes. Anything and everything. French, Dago, German, American, all kinds. Anything and everything. Spanish and all. All nations. Yeah.
Where did you have the parade? Where did you march? Where did you have that? Downtown near Spain?
Yes. Oh, yeah. All around the neighborhood. Your home. All around the neighborhood, yeah.
When, we lived on Charton, Mandeville, is when he used to have Raymond Hickey and his sons played with him then, too.
That's where I, that's where I had the most of my rehearsals.
You had all the rehearsals there.
Most of them.
Mandeville and Charton.
Yeah. Mandeville and Charton. Yeah.
I think Dr. Sushon took some pictures of the house.

That's right. That's right. We lived in there many a year. He was a basement. We lived in there for many a many years. And that's where I had my rehearsals. Yeah. It's such a fine place. Beautiful basement, you know. Beautiful. See? I had my rehearsals. Everything that I had in there. I was right on then till War I. That's all.
Yeah.

That's all. Now, Dune, as I believe I've explained it to you once before, during the Spanish and American War, I had 15 pieces that really could play bugle and piccolo and drums. Where's my picture? You got it there?
I think you showed us that picture last week when we were here with the man from Germany.
That's right, yeah. Now, when they were getting ready to go across, Armistice again, stopped us from going. They had a beautiful band. Bugle, piccoloos, and drums.
Were you playing ragtime music at that time too? What? Played ragtime music. In 1898 at the Spanish American War at that time?
Yeah.
Played music.
But here, we never played no ragtime in this band. No,
I know.
Oh, no. What an art.
No. But you did play the dance music.
Oh, yes, we had dance music that time, yeah. But we played not in that, but military. What do you mean? This here?
That one?
Yeah, that's one picture you showed us.
That's one,
but he's got one by itself that missed the...

Let me tell you about this thing. I took that whole group out to the city park. Oh, yeah, there's the trees out there. And they got messed up with a whole lot of gals out there. Holy, they wouldn't, none of them would come and take their pictures if they were with them girls. They wouldn't come and take their pictures. You only had six
in the picture, huh? Yeah.
Huh?
Only six people in the picture. Only six in this picture.
That's all, yeah. That's all. They were out with them girls having a good time.
You had the, had the picture like this by itself.
You remember? Yes, I saw that.
Last week, yeah.
I don't remember. Of course, them girls had lunch and all with them, you know. They went with them because they were getting their lunch.

And that was the one of the Spanish-American war. That's it. Yeah. That's it. Yeah. Yeah. That's it. Are there any other men that played with you later? No. No. No. In the ragtime band? No. All of them.
No. Canna-lade, Daisy.
The only one I know is Gosher.
I don't know none of them. No. No. No.
This fellow's Adolph Gosher.

No, no. No one. That's a drum and bugle. Adolph never played with me. No. No. Here's something I organized, reorganized in 1936. I built that hook and ladder. And it's standing out there today in the yard. It's right there standing out in the yard.
Is that the one that's up at the protection levee?
Yeah.
Way uptown, Carlton? It's covered where over there was cut top over there. It's covered over there with top over there. We're talking to that chat. That's it.
That's a hook and ladder.
Don't tip on the head.
They had it up in the French quarters. We had it up in the French quarters. Straighted here not so long ago in the French quarters with it. I think I saw that. Horse drawn. It's a horse drawn outfit.
Yeah, I saw that once.
That's it. That's the same one.
I had that picture. I had it last week or so when we was here. But them boys was
here. Just the individual picture.
Yeah, by itself. Yeah, I remember. I remember. I remember. I remember.
Let me just ask you one more question about funerals. You said you played with the... Did you ever play on this side of the river?
The funerals. Did you ever play on this side of the river?
Playing funerals? For funerals? No. Brookhoven and that fellow used to have that job. William J. Braun, Brookhoven.
They played on this side. You were on the other side then?
All my funerals, most of the funerals I played, that is all of them.
Yeah.

Was for, you say from, you would say from Algiers up into West Wigo. All the funerals over there. None on this side. Because they used to play all that funerals. It seemed, I don't know, they had some agreement, some contracts in there with these organizations. See, these men did, you understand? And of course, had to hire them in case of the funerals. Now, me, well, of course, I never had no contract with none of them and no agreements with none of them. And if they died, they wanted my band, they wanted us to ban. See?

You see, this band, that's the first band that ever played on the air, over the air. W-O-W-L. You can hardly see them anymore. Who was the man? Alfred Lane. Alfred Lane, he had that, and Jimmy Cousins and Marlowe and Bud Lawyer-Kaner was with him.
Yeah, what play? Is this the same Marlowe that helped Nick LaRocca learn his...

No, that's his brother. That's his brother. This fellow plays trombone, but the other, his brother played cornet, yeah. Manuel. Yeah. I had some of them pictures. I believe they're wrapped up. They're not... Yeah, that's the first band that ever played over the air.
Yeah, over the air. Say what that was about what... This is Johnny Root.
No, you can't read the date.
No, it's a pity.
That's what she done wrong. She never dates these things. They should date them.
Yeah, but it's been nice.
The ones I had was all dated.
Is that dated? It was dated, but I guess... That's so long.
Faded off of them.
Yeah.
All that stuff that I had put away, the roaches and mice and all got into it in the shed. I had to burn it. I had all that stuff almost dated. Up to the time, where, when, and how?
How long ago was it since you burned it, Dad?
Who that?
How long since you
burned it? How long ago since you burned it? Oh, I burned that
a long time ago. Oh, boy, a good while ago. A long time ago, yeah.
A long time ago.
You see...
This is from 1934.

I built this place, you understand? 1934. I lived in it a while, you see. And I built another place in Florida Walk and... Florida Walk and... Not Montague. Cluitt. Florida Walk and Cluitt right over the bridge. The place behind there. Oh. Florida Walk and Cluitt. That's when she destroyed the whole lot of that place. Oh, yeah.
When we moved back there.

See? Yeah. I moved out of here because I had a French friend of mine who was to move out of here. and he would like to move in here. And after he moved, I kept this place empty for three or four solid years. I had that picture last week when you was here. I got rid of that place in Florida Walk. I actually give it away to keep a fella from being sent back to Germany. Yeah. Yeah. I think it was in this... I moved back in here then. See?
It must have been... Did you ever know any other bands that played across the river there, Jack? Did you know of any other bands that played over on the other side?
You know any other band that played over the river? Fisher played over there, didn't he?
Johnny Fisher played there not much. No. I don't know. I thought he would. No, I don't. Outside of Johnny Fisher. No. I don't.
Did you ever hear of a band, a colored band over there by the name of Minetta Band?
Who?
A Minetta. Minetta Band. A man by the name of Norman Minetta.
Norman Minetta Band over the river?
No. No. You may as well say I was raised over the river. I never heard of it.
There was another piano teacher that taught all instruments named Divergis. Did you know him?
Who?
Divergis. Divergis. Divergis.
Divergis?
Al Divergis.
I heard of Al Divergis. I heard of Al Divergis.
What it was, no matter what was where they needed a little music, they come and got me. No other band that seemed like had any chance.
He wasn't in existence when this was taken.
I don't believe it. Nick wasn't playing when the Biloxi band. Yeah.
That's the Biloxi band, no. You got Martin Korn, you got Denny Stevens, and two coachmans, and Kendall.
Them boys were all dead.
And Kendall. All of them are dead. Yeah, they're dead, I know. Emil Christian is with you there, too. Yeah.
This is all before the time that Nick ever played.
Oh, yeah. That's before the time. Oh, yeah. That's before his time, yeah. They have three bands over there. I should have had the date on this.
I'm going to ask you about these advertising jobs. About what year would that be, when you played an advertising?
I don't know. What year was that advertising? You don't remember, huh?
Search me, I ain't got your dog.
Let's see what the wagon looks like. It's one of the old furniture. Can you read that sign, anyone, there? No, let me hold it up. I have a new one. Two heart dancing. Jackson Hall. Ray here.
Ray in that band.
Yeah.
Jackson Hall.
Jackson Hall. Jackson Hall.
Yeah, that's the Mike Shack place. Down here.
Jackson Hall.
Congress and Burgundy.
Congress and Burgundy. That was the hall. I don't remember.
Yeah. Congress and Burgundy. Jackson Hall. Oh, yeah. They were going to play a dance there that night.
They used to have. Yeah. They had a dancing school there. Three times a week. They had a dancing school. Yeah.
Six, seven. There's ten fellows all together here, I believe. One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten. Counting the driver. Yeah. And two horses.
I used to do advertising for them, too, you know, and wagons and everything else, you know.
That's Johnny Pijol here.
Yeah.
He used to play pickled clarinet with you.
Standing there for the case. Right here.
Johnny played clarinet. That's Pijol. I don't remember none of them. I'll tell you the truth.
I don't, really.
It's a shame. They should have had. They should have been dated. That would have been the best. That's the same one for me. That would have been your best bet.
Yeah, that's the same one in the park. Now, what's this? This in the bar room, huh?
Yeah, that's in the bar room over the river, yeah. Oh, that's across the river? You remember Captain Willie Pearson?
Yeah.
That's him.
Which bar room is that, then?
What bar room is that?
A spirit, a doublehead. A spirit before your time on Decatur Street by the market.
Oh.
A wine joint.
Oh, that's it, huh?
I made out I was a barkeeper in there. Ah, yeah, I see. Behind the bar.
Yeah.
A wine joint. Doublehead. They used to call him doublehead.
You remember Captain William Peterson, don't you? That's him.
I don't remember about him, but...
You heard of him, Captain William Peterson? That's him. That's him.
Oh, that's way before your time.
I don't... Yeah, I think we've talked about this, the David Coggett number one picture, yeah. Who's in the blacksmith? That's him.
That's him.
Oh, Jack's the blacksmith, huh? Was that the shop?
And this is Frank Christian here.
Now there's Frank Christian, too.
That's Frank Christian there. When do you do that happen, too?
Running back of the wheel. I built that truck you see out there. Yeah, that's Frank Christian, yeah. 36. I built that hook and ladder that's out there.
Where was this shop, Jack?
Wasn't that on Charter Street?
This is on Charter between Manavon and Maroney, on the riverside of the Banker, where the stocking mill is today.
Oh, yeah. Yeah, yeah.

Is that where you made your drum beater? In that shop? Yeah, right there. Is that right? That's where you made it, huh? These traps. Yeah, that's fine. I think this big picture here with Dave Perkins was shown in a book, Jazz Men. Yeah. And they divided the picture up. They didn't show the whole picture. They showed Dave Perkins and the man sitting down with the alto or baritone. Yeah, Blasco. And then they showed a single one over here on the other side, I believe, with Jack standing. I don't think the whole picture was there. No.
Yeah, we had loaned those pictures to somebody.
I don't know. I think Charles Smith reproduced part of that.
Yeah.
This funny one here with the little tiny...
Them days, they used to have wagons all around Connaughtry delivering packages.
You know, they're like, they have the trucks. It used to be wagons.
No automobiles enough for trucks or anything. Deliveries. All horse stuff.
For those stores.
And I used to do all their work, pretty much. Yeah. Blacksmith and play music, too.
